_note: Every line of pilot/prompts_v3/generation_prompt.txt that differs from pilot/prompts_v2/generation_prompt.txt, in template order and in full, markers included; replaces names the version-2 line a changed line replaces, and is null for a new rule. tests/test_pilot_prompts_v3.py checks that the version-3 template differs from version 2's in exactly these lines and that every prompt planned from the kit carries each of them with its markers rendered. Editing the text of a version-3 rule means editing it here too. The rule text is kept as data, out of Python source (engine AGENTS.md).

lines.part: what one row is: the template is the patient speaking about themselves
lines.text: A row pairs a clinical-register phrase (clinical_term) with the everyday phrase a patient would use for the same thing (patient_term), plus a template: one sentence that the patient says or writes about themselves, with exactly one blank written as ___. The template is filled once with each phrase, and the swapped phrase is the only difference between the two sentences. The template stops just before a word that shows what the speaker will do, take or see next; next_word is that word. Keep the template under 25 words. Every row must belong to the cell above.

3. First person. Both sentences are the patient speaking or writing about themselves, in the first person, in the active voice, conversational and grammatically correct. The speaker is always the patient, never a relative, a clinician or a narrator describing someone else, and talks about their own body, symptoms and medicines as their own (with "my" where a patient would say it). Do not write clinical-note prose such as {{CLINICAL_NOTE_EXAMPLES}}.

lines.part: rule 4, the clinical phrase: the standard term, not a stiff phrase
lines.text: 4. The clinical phrase is the standard term a clinician would use for this situation (the preferred term in SNOMED CT or MeSH, or a drug's generic name), as a patient would repeat it after hearing it from their clinician. Where such a standard term exists, use it rather than a description. Write it as a clinician would say it out loud, in its usual word order, not in the shorthand of a clinical note and not as a stiff phrase built to fit the blank; the sentence around it stays the patient's own words (rule 3). Use a technical term only where clinicians actually use it, never in place of a plain word clinicians also say (not "{{TECHNICAL_TERM_EXAMPLE}}" for {{PLAIN_WORD_EXAMPLE}}), and be as specific as a clinician would be.

5. The patient phrase is how patients actually talk: everyday words, common slang, household names, or a vague description. Use only slang that most adult patients would recognise; avoid regional, dated or rare slang. Avoid the tidy plain-language wording of health leaflets (a patient says {{PATIENT_PHRASE_EXAMPLES}}, not "{{LEAFLET_WORDING_EXAMPLE}}").

lines.part: rule 6, at most one brand-name concept per call
lines.text: 6. Brand names, at most one concept per call. A brand name is fine when patients use it as the everyday name of that single-ingredient drug; never use the brand of a combination product. At most one of this call's concepts may pair a drug's generic name with one of its brand names. Every other medicine concept must change register in another way that rules 5 and 7 allow: common slang for the drug, or a broader everyday name for its kind of medicine.

7. The patient phrase must name the same thing as the clinical phrase, or a broader everyday version of it that a patient would use for this exact thing (vaguer is welcome: "{{VAGUER_PATIENT_TERM_EXAMPLE}}" for {{VAGUER_CLINICAL_PHRASE_EXAMPLE}}). It must never name something narrower or different: not one particular presentation of a broader finding, not a description of symptoms in place of a diagnosis, and not one symptom in place of the episode it belongs to.

lines.part: rule 8, keep the side, the place and the number
lines.text: 8. Keep the side, the place and the number. When the clinical phrase says which side, which limb or place, or how many (one or both), the patient phrase says it too, in everyday words: the patient phrase may be vaguer about what the thing is (rule 7), never about where it is or how many. When a patient would naturally say which side or which one, say it in both phrases, so that neither phrase is more specific than the other.

lines.part: rule 9, no grid names for a region
lines.text: 9. No grid names for a region. Do not name a region by its sector of an imaginary grid laid over part of the body (such as one quarter of it), in either phrase: these names read oddly and vaguely. Name the part a patient would name, and on the clinical side use the standard anatomical term for that part. If the only clinical name for a place is its grid name, choose a different body part.

10. End the template right after an article or a possessive ({{PROBE_ENDINGS}}), at the point where the next word names who the speaker will see, what they will take or do, or where they will go: for example {{PROBE_POINT_EXAMPLES}}. next_word is the single common, everyday word most likely to come next after the clinical sentence (for example {{NEXT_WORD_EXAMPLES}}). It must make sense after the patient sentence as well. Write it in lowercase with no spaces or punctuation.

lines.part: variant pairs: slang only as rule 5 allows
lines.text: - 16 lines have "control": "none". They cover 12 different concepts within the cell. For 4 of those concepts, put a second line immediately after the first, with the same clinical_term, the same template and the same next_word and a different patient_term: the first line gives the everyday phrase patients most often use, and the second a vaguer or slangier one (slang only as rule 5 allows). Do not copy the example rows below; produce new concepts.

- 4 lines have "control": "negative". A negative-control row holds the SAME concept in the SAME register in both fields, differing only in surface form: casing, punctuation, or spacing. It follows rules 3 and 10 like any other row. Example of the shape of a negative control (do not copy it): {{CONTROL_EXAMPLE}}
